Types of Bank Accounts in India: Savings, Current, FD, RD and NRI

Banks offer accounts for everyday money, for businesses, for savings over time, and for non-residents. This guide compares them, and explains how money moves between them.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Demand and time deposits

Banks' deposits fall into two broad groups. Demand deposits, such as savings and current accounts, can be withdrawn whenever you like. Time deposits, such as fixed deposits and recurring deposits, are placed for an agreed period at a higher rate.

The main accounts compared

AccountForInterestKey feature
Savings accountIndividualsModestEveryday money, easy withdrawals
Salary accountEmployeesAs for savingsOften no minimum balance while salary is credited
Basic savings (BSBDA)EveryoneAs for savingsNo minimum balance, with basic services

Fixed depositLump-sum saversHigher, and fixedSet period, penalty if closed early

AccountHoldsRepatriableInterest taxed in India

FCNR(B)Foreign currency term depositFullyNo

Useful bank facilities

  • Auto-sweep: surplus above a limit moves into an FD on its own and comes back when required, so idle balance earns more while staying available.
  • Overdraft: withdraw beyond your balance up to a limit, paying interest only on what you use. It may be secured against an FD.
  • Cash credit: a working-capital limit for businesses, against stock and receivables.
  • Standing instruction or auto-debit: automatic payments, such as for an RD or SIP.
  • Locker: safe storage, which is rented and is not a deposit.

MethodSpeedTypical use

How banks make money

A bank earns the gap between what it charges borrowers and what it pays depositors, which is called net interest margin, plus fee income. It must hold part of its deposits as CRR and SLR, so it cannot lend every rupee. Loans that stop paying become NPAs, which hurt profits.

Deposit safety

DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including principal and interest. This covers savings, current, fixed and recurring deposits with insured banks. Corporate deposits with companies and NBFCs are not covered. Check the DICGC website for the current limit.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between a savings and a current account?

A savings account is for individuals and pays interest. A current account is for businesses with many transactions, usually pays no interest and can include an overdraft.

What is the difference between NRE and NRO accounts?

NRE holds foreign earnings, is fully repatriable and its interest is tax-free in India. NRO holds income earned in India, has repatriation limits and its interest is taxable.

What is the difference between NEFT and RTGS?

NEFT settles in batches and has no minimum amount. RTGS settles each payment in real time and is meant for ₹2 lakh and above.
